citation.title: Confidence Intervals for Linear Unbiased Estimators under Constrained Dependence

standing_assumptions:
The article is Electronic Journal of Statistics 12 (2018) 2238–2252. Printed page = PDF page + 2237 (printed p. 2240 is PDF p. 3). Everything quoted from the article was read from the page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png, re-rendered at 200 dpi for the formulas).
(S1) Graph and dependency graph. p. 2240 (PDF p. 3): "Consider a simple graph $\mathcal G = (\mathcal V, \mathcal E)$ with no parallel edges or self-loops. Let $|\mathcal V| = N$. Associated with each vertex $i \in \mathcal V$ is a random variable $Y_i$, and $\mathcal G$ characterizes probabilistic dependencies in the outcomes [e.g., 3]." "Definition 1 (Dependency graph). $\mathcal G$ is a dependency graph if for all disjoint sets $\mathcal V_1, \mathcal V_2 \subset \mathcal V$ with no edge in $\mathcal E$ connecting a vertex in $\mathcal V_1$ to a vertex in $\mathcal V_2$, the set $\{Y_i : i \in \mathcal V_1\}$ is independent from the set $\{Y_j : j \in \mathcal V_2\}$."
(S2) Observation. p. 2240 (PDF p. 3): "Suppose $\mathcal G$ is a dependency graph and we observe a subset $\mathcal V_S \subseteq \mathcal V$, where $|\mathcal V_S| = n$. Label these observed vertices $1, \ldots, n$, and label the unobserved vertices in $\mathcal V \setminus \mathcal V_S$ arbitrarily by $n+1, \ldots, N$. For each $i \in \mathcal V_S$, we observe the outcomes $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$, a fixed vector of coefficients $\theta = \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n$, and the degrees $d_i = |\{j : \{i,j\} \in \mathcal E\}|$ for each $i \in \mathcal V_S$." "Definition 2 (Induced subgraph). For a set of vertices $\mathcal V_S \subseteq \mathcal V$, the induced subgraph in $\mathcal G$ is $\mathcal G_S = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_S)$, where $\mathcal E_S = \{\{i,j\} : i \in \mathcal V_S,\ j \in \mathcal V_S,\ \text{and } \{i,j\} \in \mathcal E\}$." "Let $\mathcal G_S = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_S)$ be the induced subgraph of the observed vertices $\mathcal V_S$. It follows that $\mathcal G_S$ is also a dependency graph. Let $\mathcal G_R = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_R)$ be a subgraph of $\mathcal G_S$, consisting of all the observed vertices in $\mathcal V_S$, and a subset of the edges in $\mathcal E_S$." "Assumption 1 (Observed data). We observe the random outcomes $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$, the fixed degrees $d_1, \ldots, d_n$, the fixed coefficients $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n$, and the fixed recruitment graph $\mathcal G_R$." "Let $Y = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $d = (d_1, \ldots, d_n)$, and denote the observed data as $Z = (Y, d, \theta, \mathcal G_R)$."
(S3) Estimator and target. p. 2240 (PDF p. 3): "Definition 3 (Linear unbiased estimator (LUE)). An estimator $\hat\beta$ is a linear unbiased estimator (LUE) of $\beta$ if $\hat\beta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S} \theta_i Y_i$ where $\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta] = \beta$." p. 2241 (PDF p. 4): "In what follows, we wish to conduct inference on $\beta$ given $Z$. We proceed by constructing conservative estimators of $\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}^{n}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S}^{n} \theta_i\theta_j\,\mathrm{cov}(Y_i, Y_j)$."
(S4) Compatible adjacency matrices. p. 2241 (PDF p. 4): "We consider a class of variance estimators that depend on knowledge of $\mathcal G_S$, whose structure is represented by an $n \times n$ binary symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix in which rows and columns are ordered by the indices $1, \ldots, n$ of the vertices in $\mathcal V_S$." "Definition 4 (Compatibility). The $n \times n$ binary symmetric adjacency matrix $A$ is compatible with the observed data $Z$ if for each $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_R$, $A_{ij} = A_{ji} = 1$, and for each $i \in \mathcal V_S$, $\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A_{ij} \le d_i$." "The last condition in Definition 4 requires that the degree of $i$ in the subgraph $\mathcal G_S$ not be greater than its degree in the full graph $\mathcal G$. Let $A^{\mathcal O} = \{A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}\}$ be the true $n \times n$ adjacency matrix of $\mathcal G_S$, where $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} = 1$ if $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_S$ for $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ and 0 otherwise. Let $\mathcal A(Z) = \{A : A \text{ is compatible with } Z\}$ in the sense of Definition 4; it is clear that $A^{\mathcal O} \in \mathcal A(Z)$." "Definition 5 (Oracle estimator). For a family of variance estimators $\widehat V(A;Z)$ defined for $A \in \mathcal A(Z)$, the oracle estimator is $\widehat V(A^{\mathcal O};Z)$." "For a variance estimator $\widehat V(A;Z)$, define the set $\mathcal A^m = \{A \in \mathcal A(Z) : \widehat V(A;Z) \text{ is maximized}\}$." "Definition 6 (Maximal compatible estimator). Let $A^m \in \mathcal A^m$. The maximal compatible estimator is $\widehat V(A^m;Z)$."
(S5) Asymptotic scaling. p. 2242 (PDF p. 5): "Assumption 2 (Asymptotic scaling). Consider the sequence $(\mathcal G, Z)_n$ of nested graphs $\mathcal G$ and observed data $Z = (\mathcal G_R, Y, d)$, where $\mathcal G_R = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_R)$, $|\mathcal V_S| = n$, and $|\mathcal V| = N_n \ge n$. Assume there exist finite, positive constants $c_1$, $c_2$ such that for every element $(\mathcal G, Z)_n$, $\Pr(|\theta_i Y_i - \beta| > c_1) = 0, \forall i \in \mathcal V_S$ (bounded outcome values) and $\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} \le c_2, \forall i \in \mathcal V_S$ (bounded degrees in dependency graph). Further assume there exists a finite, positive constant $c_3$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = c_3$ (nondegenerate limiting variance). Finally, assume $c_4$ is a finite positive constant such that $|\theta_i| < c_4$."
(S6) General estimator. p. 2242 (PDF p. 5): "Define the plug-in sample variance $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = n^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}(\theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta)^2$, and the estimator $\widehat V_1(A;Z) = \frac{1}{n^2}\left[n\hat\sigma_\theta^2 + \sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A_{ij}(\theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta)(\theta_j Y_j - \hat\beta)\right]$. (3.1)" p. 2244 (PDF p. 7): "Let $\mathcal A_1^m = \{A \in \mathcal A(Z) : \widehat V_1(A;Z) \text{ is maximized}\}$ be the set of compatible adjacency matrices that maximize $\widehat V_1(A;Z)$. Let $\Theta = \mathrm{diag}(\theta)$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with $\Theta_{ii} = \theta_i$ and $\Theta_{ij} = 0$ for $i \ne j$."
(S7) Homoskedastic estimators. p. 2246 (PDF p. 9): "Assumption 3 (Homoskedasticity). $\mathrm{var}(\theta_i Y_i) = \mathrm{var}(\theta_j Y_j), \forall i, j \in \mathcal V$." "A bound that is relatively computationally simple to compute can be derived by noting that when $\mathrm{var}(\theta_i Y_i) = \sigma_\theta^2$, $\mathrm{cov}(\theta_i Y_i, \theta_j Y_j) \le \sigma_\theta^2 A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}$. Define the estimator $\widehat V_2(A;Z) = \frac{\hat\sigma_\theta^2}{n}\left[1 + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A_{ij}\right]$. (3.7)" "Define $\mathcal A_2^m = \{A \in \mathcal A(Z) : \widehat V_2(A;Z) \text{ is maximized}\}$, and let $A^m \in \mathcal A_2^m$." pp. 2246–2247 (PDF pp. 9–10): "For $i \in \mathcal V_S$, let $d_i' = \min\{d_i, n-1\}$ be the degree of $i$ in $\mathcal G$, truncated at $n-1$. Let $\widehat V_2'(Z) = \frac{\hat\sigma_\theta^2}{n}\left[1 + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S} d_i'\right]$. (3.9)"
(S8) Degree bounds in place of degrees. p. 2248 (PDF p. 11): "Alternatively, we may not have full knowledge of the degrees $d = (d_1, \ldots, d_n)$, and instead have only an upper bound $d_i^*$ for each $d_i$, or a global upper bound $d_i \le d^*$ for all $i = 1, \ldots, n$. Conservative variance estimation in both of these cases can be achieved (by substituting $d_i^*$ or $d^*$ for $d_i$) with no change to the programs (3.5) and (3.8) or to the asymptotic results given here. When no information about $\mathcal G_R$ or the degrees $d$ is available, setting every $d_i = d^* = n-1$ delivers a maximally conservative upper bound."
(S9) Audit notation, not in the paper (from the validators' derivations and the from-scratch check of the correction). $X_i = \theta_i Y_i$; $\mu_i = \mathrm{E}[X_i]$; $\delta_i = \mu_i - \beta$ (so $\sum_i \delta_i = 0$ by Definition 3, but no $\delta_i$ need be 0); $u_i = X_i - \mu_i$; $e_i = X_i - \hat\beta$; $C$ is the $n \times n$ covariance matrix of $(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$; $S = I + A^{\mathcal O}$; $b_n = \frac{1}{n}\delta^{\mathsf T}(I + A^{\mathcal O})\delta = \frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_i \delta_i^2 + \sum_i\sum_j A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}\delta_i\delta_j\right]$; for a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $M$, $\widehat V_M = \frac{1}{n^2}e^{\mathsf T}Me$, so that $\widehat V_1(A;Z) = \widehat V_{I+A}$; for an adjacency matrix $A$, $d_i^A = \sum_j A_{ij}$ and $D_A = \mathrm{diag}(d_i^A)$; $D' = \mathrm{diag}(d_i')$. By Definition 1, $C_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \ne j$ and $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} = 0$, so $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\mathrm{tr}\{(I + A^{\mathcal O})C\}$.
(S10) Reading conventions (for the formalizer; conventions, not quotations). (a) At each $n$ there is one probability space carrying the outcomes; $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{var}$, $\mathrm{cov}$, $\Pr$ refer to their joint law. The graphs, the degrees $d_i$ and the coefficients $\theta_i$ are non-random; they and $\beta = \mathrm{E}[\hat\beta]$ may depend on $n$ (the regression weights of Section 2 do). (b) The constants $c_1, \ldots, c_4$ of Assumption 2 do not depend on $n$, and its conditions hold for every $n$ and every $i \in \mathcal V_S$. (c) "$\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(\cdot > \epsilon) = 0$ for any $\epsilon > 0$" is a statement about the sequence indexed by $n$. (d) "will have (at least) $100(1-\alpha)\%$ coverage for $\beta$ in large $n$" is read as: the limit (limit inferior) of $\Pr(|\hat\beta - \beta| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat V})$ equals (is at least) $1 - \alpha$, for $0 < \alpha < 1$, with $z_{1-\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)$. The printed interval is undefined when $\widehat V < 0$, which can happen for $\widehat V_1$; the corrected statements use $\max\{\widehat V, 0\}$. (e) Double sums over $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ are over ordered pairs. (f) In (3.5), $\Theta Y - \hat\beta$ is the vector with entries $\theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta$, $1$ is the vector of ones, and $\preceq$, $\succeq$ are element-wise $\le$, $\ge$ (the print says "less-than"; P011-N001). (g) Assumption 3 is used only for $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ (P011-N001); the common variance, which may depend on $n$, is written $\sigma_\theta^2$ in the paper and $\sigma_n^2$ in the corrected statements. (h) "Valid constraints" means $\mathcal E_R \subseteq \mathcal E_S$ and $d_i \ge \sum_j A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}$ for every $i \in \mathcal V_S$ (true degrees in $\mathcal G$, or upper bounds on them as in (S8)), which gives $A^{\mathcal O} \in \mathcal A(Z)$. (i) In Corollaries 1 and 3, $A^m \in \mathcal A_1^m$; in Lemma 1 and Corollaries 2 and 4, $A^m \in \mathcal A_2^m$.
Scope of the list. Targets come from two sources. (1) Headline claims P011-H1 to P011-H7 are mathematical and are targets (H1 and H4 are false as printed and appear as results touched by P011-E001; H2, H3, H5, H6 and the formal part of H7 appear as headline results). P011-H8 (the R package implements the method) is a statement about software and is not a target. (2) Confirmed errors whose correction changes a mathematical statement, a formula or a proof step: P011-E001 (Critical; targets T1–T10, T31–T33, with the corrected statements taken from the from-scratch check runs/P011/correction-recheck/recheck.json, as NOTES-FOR-AGENTS.md directs), P011-E004 (Moderate; T11, T12, T34), P011-E002 (Moderate; T13, T14, T30), P011-N006 (Moderate; an interpretive finding about the package vignette and README that rests on an exact counterexample; T15, T16, T35), and the Minor errors P011-E003 (T17, T18), P011-E005 (T19, T20), P011-E006 (T21), P011-E007 (T22, T23), P011-N001 (T24) and P011-E015 (T25, T26; the package's variance helpers use divisor $n-1$ where the paper's formulas (3.1), (3.7), (3.9) use $n$, a wrong constant relative to the printed formulas). Not targets: P011-E009 and P011-N007 (misprinted words), P011-N002 (bibliography), P011-E011, P011-E013 and P011-E014 (the package stops with an error or does not check the solver status: no formula or statement to correct), P011-E012 (the help page and vignette name estimator (3.9) where the code returns (3.7) at the optimized graph; both formulas and Lemma 1, which relates them, are correct as printed and are target T28, so there is no mathematical statement to correct), P011-E010 (out of scope), P011-E008 (clarity note), P011-N003 and P011-N008 (undetermined), P011-N004 and P011-N005 (not confirmed).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 2, the consistency claimed for the auxiliary oracle estimator $\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z)$, as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed proof step refuted, p. 2246] "As in the proof of Proposition 1, $\hat\sigma_\theta^2$ converges in mean square. By Assumption 2, $1 \le 1 + \frac1n\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S}A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} \le 1 + c_2$, allowing us to invoke Slutsky's Theorem and Chebyshev's Inequality to show $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(|n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) - n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta)| < \epsilon) = 0$." The step is refuted both as printed and in the intended reading with $> \epsilon$ (consistency of $n\widehat V_2^*$ for $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta)$).
[Counterexample, from the validator] Let $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots$ be independent with $\Pr(\varepsilon_i = 1) = \Pr(\varepsilon_i = -1) = 1/2$; $\mu_i = 2$ for odd $i$ and $\mu_i = 0$ for even $i$; $Y_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i$. At sample size $n$ put $p = \lceil n/2\rceil$, $r = p - \lfloor n/2\rfloor \in \{0, 1\}$, $t_n = n/(2p)$, $\theta_i = t_n$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, $X_i = t_nY_i$, $\beta = 1$. $\mathcal G$ is the edgeless graph on $\{1, \ldots, n\}$, every vertex is observed ($N_n = n$), $\mathcal E_R = \emptyset$, $A^{\mathcal O} = 0$, $d_i = 0$.
(a) [The hypotheses hold.] $\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta] = t_n \cdot 2p/n = 1 = \beta$ for every $n$. $1/2 \le t_n \le 1$ and $|X_i - 1| \le 2$ ($c_1 = 2$). All degrees are 0 ($c_2 = 1$). $\mathrm{var}(X_i) = t_n^2 =: \sigma_n^2$ for every $i$ (Assumption 3). $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = t_n^2 \to 1$ ($c_3 = 1$). $|\theta_i| \le 1 < 2$ ($c_4 = 2$). The raw outcomes and the graphs are nested.
(b) Because $A^{\mathcal O} = 0$, $n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) = n\widehat V_2(A^{\mathcal O};Z) = \hat\sigma_\theta^2$, whatever the correlations.
(c) [Exact decomposition.] With $\delta_i = t_n\mu_i - 1$, $M_n = \frac1n\sum_i\delta_i^2 = t_n^2\left(1 - \frac{r^2}{n^2}\right)$, $S_n = \sum_i\varepsilon_i$ and $H_n = \sum_i\delta_i\varepsilon_i$: $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = \sigma_n^2 + M_n + \frac{2t_nH_n}{n} - \frac{t_n^2S_n^2}{n^2}$. With $R_n = \hat\sigma_\theta^2 - (\sigma_n^2 + M_n)$: $\mathrm{E}[R_n] = -\frac{\sigma_n^2}{n}$ and $\mathrm{E}[R_n^2] = \frac{4\sigma_n^2M_n}{n} + \sigma_n^4\left(\frac{3}{n^2} - \frac{2}{n^3}\right)$.
(d) [The limit.] $D_n := n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) - n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = M_n + R_n \to 1$ in probability. For even $n$: $t_n = 1$, $M_n = 1$, $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = 1$, $n\widehat V_2^* = 2 + \frac{2T_n}{n} - \frac{S_n^2}{n^2}$ with $T_n = \sum_i(-1)^{i+1}\varepsilon_i$, and $\mathrm{E}[(D_n - 1)^2] = \frac4n + \frac{3}{n^2} - \frac{2}{n^3}$.
(e) [Both readings fail.] $\Pr(|D_n| > 1/2) \ge 1 - 4\mathrm{E}[(D_n - 1)^2] \to 1$ along even $n$, so the consistency reading fails; and $\Pr(|D_n| < 3/2) \ge 1 - 4\mathrm{E}[(D_n - 1)^2] \to 1$, so the display as printed fails at $\epsilon = 3/2$.
(f) [Proposition 2 itself is not contradicted.] In this example $\Pr(n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) - n\widehat V_2(A^{\mathcal O};Z) > 1/2) \to 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Assumptions 2, 3 and (3.7): standing assumptions (S5), (S7). The auxiliary estimator $\widehat V_2^*$ is defined only in the printed proof, transcribed in P011-T34; its correlations are printed $\rho_i$ (P011-E006), which does not matter here because $A^{\mathcal O} = 0$. $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = \frac1n\sum_i(X_i - \hat\beta)^2$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each $n$. (1) $\sum_i\delta_i = 0$ and $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = \frac1n\sum_i(X_i - 1)^2 - (\hat\beta - 1)^2 = \frac1n\sum_i(\delta_i + t_n\varepsilon_i)^2 - \frac{t_n^2S_n^2}{n^2}$. (2) $\mathrm{E}[S_n^2] = n$, $\mathrm{E}[S_n^4] = 3n^2 - 2n$, $\mathrm{E}[H_n] = 0$, $\mathrm{E}[H_n^2] = nM_n$, $\mathrm{E}[H_nS_n^2] = 0$ (sign-reversal symmetry). (3) The empirical variance of the alternating $\mu_i$ is $1 - r^2/n^2$. (4) Exact values from the validator's enumeration: $n = 2$: $\Pr(|D_n| > 1/2) = 1/2$, $\Pr(|D_n| < 3/2) = 3/4$, $\Pr(n\,\mathrm{var} - n\widehat V_2 > 1/2) = 1/4$; $n = 4$: $5/8$, $11/16$, $1/16$; $n = 8$: $85/128$, $219/256$, $9/256$; $\mathrm{E}[n\widehat V_2^*] = 3/2, 7/4, 15/8$ at $n = 2, 4, 8$. (5) Markov's inequality applied to $(D_n - 1)^2$ for (e).
canonical_claim.note: The weights depend on n only through t_n and equal 1 at every even n; the validator reads "fixed coefficients" as non-random at each n, as in the paper's regression example. Unequal means do not always break the auxiliary consistency: with mu_1 = 2, mu_2 = 0 and mu_i = 1 for i >= 3 (theta = 1 for n >= 2), M_n = 2/n and E[(n V2* - n var)^2] = 11/n^2 - 2/n^3, which tends to 0 (same artifact, section 4).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 2 with its proof corrected (a direct one-sided argument that replaces the auxiliary consistency step)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected statement, from the validator's repair] Proposition 2 stands as printed: given Assumptions 2 and 3, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) - n\widehat V_2(A^{\mathcal O};Z) > \epsilon) = 0$ for any $\epsilon > 0$. Its proof is replaced by the following chain, in which $X_i = \theta_i Y_i$, $\delta_i = \mathrm{E}[X_i] - \beta$, $\sigma_n^2 = \mathrm{var}(X_i)$ is the common variance at sample size $n$ (Assumption 3 for $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$), $M_n = \frac1n\sum_i\delta_i^2 \ge 0$, $g_n = 1 + \frac1n\sum_i\sum_j A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}$, $U_n = \frac1n\sum_i(X_i - \beta)^2$ and $R_n = \hat\sigma_\theta^2 - (\sigma_n^2 + M_n)$.
(i) $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = U_n - (\hat\beta - \beta)^2$; $\mathrm{E}[U_n] = \sigma_n^2 + M_n$; $\mathrm{var}(U_n) \le \frac{(1 + c_2)c_1^4}{n}$; $\mathrm{E}[(\hat\beta - \beta)^2] \le \frac{(1 + c_2)c_1^2}{n}$; $\mathrm{E}[(\hat\beta - \beta)^4] \le \frac{(1 + c_2)c_1^4}{n}$; hence $\mathrm{E}[R_n^2] \le \frac{4(1 + c_2)c_1^4}{n}$.
(ii) $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = \frac1n\sum_i\sum_j\mathrm{cov}(X_i, X_j) \le \sigma_n^2g_n$, and $1 \le g_n \le 1 + c_2$.
(iii) $n\widehat V_2(A^{\mathcal O};Z) = g_n\hat\sigma_\theta^2$, and in every realization $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) - n\widehat V_2(A^{\mathcal O};Z) \le g_n(\sigma_n^2 - \hat\sigma_\theta^2) = -g_n(M_n + R_n) \le (1 + c_2)|R_n|$.
(iv) For every $\epsilon > 0$ and every $n$: $\Pr(n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) - n\widehat V_2(A^{\mathcal O};Z) > \epsilon) \le \frac{4(1 + c_2)^3c_1^4}{n\epsilon^2}$.
The proof uses no condition on the unit means, no limit for $M_n$ or $\sigma_n^2$, no auxiliary correlations and not Proposition 1. The consistency of $n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z)$ for $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta)$ asserted in the printed proof is not claimed: it is false in general when the unit means differ (P011-T11).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Assumptions 2, 3 and (3.7): standing assumptions (S5), (S7), with reading convention (S10)(g). $\hat\sigma_\theta^2$: (S6). $\delta$: audit notation (S9).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Each of (i)–(iv) is exact for each $n$. Steps: with $W_i = X_i - \beta$, $|W_i| \le c_1$; $\mathrm{cov}(W_i^2, W_j^2) = 0$ and $\mathrm{cov}(W_i, W_j) = 0$ when $i \ne j$ and $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} = 0$; at most $n(1 + c_2)$ ordered pairs are diagonal or edges; $|\mathrm{cov}(W_i^2, W_j^2)| \le c_1^4$ and $|\mathrm{cov}(W_i, W_j)| \le c_1^2$; $|\hat\beta - \beta| \le c_1$; $(a - b)^2 \le 2a^2 + 2b^2$ with $a = U_n - \mathrm{E}[U_n]$, $b = (\hat\beta - \beta)^2$; for $i \ne j$ on an edge, $\mathrm{cov}(X_i, X_j) \le \sigma_n^2$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality; Markov's inequality applied to $R_n^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Section 5 of the validator's derivation (equations (11)-(15)); the same route is statement 140 (corrected) of runs/P011/correction-recheck/recheck.json and section 7 of its DERIVATIONS.md. Repair cost: none (no new assumption; the estimator, the estimand and the conclusion are unchanged). Lemma 1 (P011-T28) then gives Corollaries 2 and 4 (P011-T37, P011-T40) unchanged.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The complexity of programs (3.5), (3.6) and (3.8), corrected: exact solution by reduction to maximum-weight matching
canonical_claim.location: p. 2245 (PDF p. 8), the two paragraphs after program (3.6); programs (3.5) p. 2244 (PDF p. 7), (3.6) p. 2245 (PDF p. 8), (3.8) p. 2246 (PDF p. 9)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text, from the validator] "This program can be encoded as a special multidimensional knapsack instance. Its degree-incidence structure makes it a maximum-weight simple b-matching problem. After fixing mandatory edges and subtracting their incidences from the degree bounds, it admits an exact polynomial-time solution by reduction to ordinary maximum-weight matching. Program (3.8) is its unit-weight case."
[Formal content] Let $V = \{1, \ldots, n\}$, $K = \{\{i,j\} : 1 \le i < j \le n\}$, $F = \mathcal E_R \subseteq K$ the mandatory edges, $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ nonnegative integers, and $w_e$ ($e \in K$) rational weights. Problem (P): maximize $\sum_{e \in S}w_e$ over $S \subseteq K$ subject to $F \subseteq S$ and $\deg_S(i) \le d_i$ for every $i \in V$.
(a) [(P) is the paper's program.] For a binary symmetric zero-diagonal $A$ with edge set $S$ and $r_i = \theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta$: $r^{\mathsf T}Ar = 2\sum_{\{i,j\} \in S}r_ir_j$ and $1^{\mathsf T}A1 = 2|S|$. So with $w_{\{i,j\}} = r_ir_j$ the maximizers of (P) are exactly the maximizers of (3.5), equivalently of (3.6) with $\hat v_{ij} = r_ir_j$; with all $w_e = 1$ they are the maximizers of (3.8).
(b) [Mandatory edges.] Let $\bar d_i = \min\{d_i, n-1\}$, $f_i = \deg_F(i)$, $b_i = \bar d_i - f_i$ and $E = K \setminus F$. (P) is feasible if and only if $b_i \ge 0$ for all $i$. Every feasible $S$ is uniquely $F \cup T$ with $T \subseteq E$ and $\deg_T(i) \le b_i$, and $\mathrm{OPT}(\mathrm P) = C_F + \mathrm{OPT}_b$, where $C_F = \sum_{e \in F}w_e$ and $\mathrm{OPT}_b = \max\{\sum_{e \in T}w_e : T \subseteq E,\ \deg_T(i) \le b_i \text{ for all } i\}$.
(c) [The matching instance.] Assume (P) feasible. Let $q = |E|$, $L$ the least common multiple of the denominators of the $w_e$, $e \in E$ ($L = 1$ if $E = \emptyset$), $W_e = Lw_e \in \mathbb Z$ and $M = 1 + \max_{e \in E}|W_e|$ (the maximum of the empty set being 0). Let $H$ be the graph with $b_i$ slot vertices $s_{i,1}, \ldots, s_{i,b_i}$ for each $i \in V$; two gadget vertices $p_{e,i}, p_{e,j}$ for each $e = \{i,j\} \in E$; an internal edge $p_{e,i}p_{e,j}$ of weight $4M$; external edges from $p_{e,i}$ to every slot of $i$ and from $p_{e,j}$ to every slot of $j$, each of weight $2M + W_e$; and no other edges. Then $\mathrm{OPT}(\mathrm P) = C_F + \frac{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{match}}(H) - 4Mq}{2L}$, where $\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{match}}(H)$ is the maximum total weight of a matching of $H$; and for every maximum-weight matching $J$ of $H$, the set $F \cup T_J$, with $T_J$ the set of $e \in E$ both of whose gadget vertices are matched to slots, is an optimal solution of (P).
(d) [Size.] $|V(H)| = 2q + \sum_i b_i \le 2n(n-1)$ and $|E(H)| = q + \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E}(b_i + b_j) \le q(2n - 1)$.
(e) [Consequence.] Programs (3.5), (3.6) and (3.8) are solved exactly in time polynomial in the input size by any polynomial-time maximum-weight matching algorithm; if their decision versions were NP-hard, then P = NP.
(f) [Exact instances from the validator.] $n = 4$, $r = (3/2, 1/2, -1/2, -3/2)$, $w_{ij} = r_ir_j$ (so $w_{12} = w_{34} = 3/4$, $w_{13} = w_{24} = -3/4$, $w_{14} = -9/4$, $w_{23} = -1/4$). With $d = (2, 1, 2, 7)$ and $F = \{\{1,3\}, \{3,4\}\}$: $b = (1, 1, 0, 2)$, $L = 4$, $M = 10$, $q = 4$, $\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{match}}(H) = 166$, $4Mq = 160$, $\mathrm{OPT}(\mathrm P) = 3/4$, attained by $\{\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{3,4\}\}$. With $d = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and $F = \{\{1,3\}\}$: $b = (0, 1, 0, 1)$, $q = 5$, $\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{match}}(H) = 4Mq = 200$, $\mathrm{OPT}(\mathrm P) = -3/4$, attained by $F$ alone.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Programs (3.5), (3.6), (3.8) and Definition 4 are transcribed in P011-T27 and the standing assumptions. $\deg_S(i)$ is the number of edges of $S$ containing $i$. A matching of a graph is a set of edges no two of which share a vertex; its weight is the sum of its edge weights. The cap $\bar d_i$ changes no feasible set because the graph is simple. In the paper's setting (P) is always feasible because $A^{\mathcal O} \in \mathcal A(Z)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) $4M > 0$, $2M + W_e > 0$ and $4M - (2M + W_e) = 2M - W_e > 0$ for every $e \in E$, also when $w_e < 0$. (2) In a maximum-weight matching of $H$ every gadget is either matched internally (contributing $4M$) or matched to a slot at both ends (contributing $4M + 2W_e$): a gadget with no matched vertex gains $4M$ by adding its internal edge, and a gadget with exactly one external edge gains $2M - W_e$ by replacing it with the internal edge. (3) A feasible $T$ yields a matching of weight $4Mq + 2L\sum_{e \in T}w_e$ by assigning distinct slots at each vertex; conversely $T_J$ is feasible because each slot is used at most once, and $\mathrm{weight}(J) = 4Mq + 2L\sum_{e \in T_J}w_e$.
canonical_claim.note: Sections 1-6 of the validator's derivation; the two instances are in exact_witnesses.json (keys mandatory_edges_and_truncated_cap, negative_mandatory_objective). No counterexample target accompanies this finding: the printed claim is a complexity classification, which is rejected under the convention P != NP, not by an instance. The validator confirms the finding in part: encoding the program as a multidimensional knapsack instance is legitimate, and the existence of a polynomial-time approximation scheme is not refuted. The polynomial-time maximum-weight matching theorem (Edmonds) is the algorithmic premise of (e) and is not proved in the artifact.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The linear-programming relaxation of programs (3.5), (3.6) and (3.8), corrected description: an upper bound that need not be attained by a graph
canonical_claim.location: p. 2245 (PDF p. 8), after program (3.6); p. 2248 (PDF p. 11), "Upper bounds for the variance estimates can be obtained by solving a relaxed form of the programs (3.5) and (3.8)"; Appendix B, p. 2250 (PDF p. 13)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text, from the validator] "General integer-programming solvers remain an implementation option; the degree-only LP relaxation can have fractional optima and still provides an upper bound when optimized or certified."
[Formal content] The relaxation of (3.6) replaces $a_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$ by $0 \le a_{ij} \le 1$, keeping the degree constraints and $a_{ij} = 1$ for $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_R$.
(a) [Upper bound.] The optimal value $w^{\mathrm{LP}}$ of the relaxation is at least the optimal value $w^{\mathrm{IP}}$ of (3.6). Hence $\frac{1}{n^2}\left[n\hat\sigma_\theta^2 + 2w^{\mathrm{LP}}\right] \ge \widehat V_1(A^m;Z)$ with $A^m \in \mathcal A_1^m$ when $\hat v_{ij} = (\theta_iY_i - \hat\beta)(\theta_jY_j - \hat\beta)$, and $\frac{\hat\sigma_\theta^2}{n}\left[1 + \frac{2w^{\mathrm{LP}}}{n}\right] \ge \widehat V_2(A^m;Z)$ with $A^m \in \mathcal A_2^m$ when $\hat v_{ij} = 1$. The same holds with $w^{\mathrm{LP}}$ replaced by any certified upper bound on it; the objective value of an arbitrary feasible point of the relaxation is not such a bound.
(b) [The relaxation is not integral for the objective of (3.5).] Six observed units, $\theta_i = 1$, $Y = (1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1)$, $\hat\beta = 0$, every $d_i = 1$, $\mathcal E_R = \emptyset$. The weights $\hat v_{ij} = Y_iY_j$ are $1$ on the six within-sign pairs and $-1$ on the nine cross-sign pairs. $w^{\mathrm{IP}} = 2$ (for example the edges $\{1,2\}$ and $\{4,5\}$), so the optimum of (3.5) is 4. $w^{\mathrm{LP}} = 3$, attained by $a_{ij} = 1/2$ on the six within-sign pairs and 0 elsewhere, and bounded above by $\sum_e\hat v_ea_e \le \sum_e a_e = \frac12\sum_i\deg_a(i) \le \frac12\sum_i d_i = 3$; the relaxed optimum of (3.5) is 6. Formula (3.1) gives $\widehat V_1 = (6 + 4)/36 = 5/18$ at the integer optimum and $(6 + 6)/36 = 1/3$ at the relaxed optimum.
(c) [The same for (3.8).] Three units with $d = (1, 1, 1)$ and $\mathcal E_R = \emptyset$: the optimum of (3.8) is $1^{\mathsf T}A1 = 2$ (one edge), and the optimum of its relaxation is 3 ($a_{12} = a_{13} = a_{23} = 1/2$; adding the three degree constraints gives $2\sum_e a_e \le 3$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Programs (3.5), (3.6), (3.8): P011-T27. (3.1), (3.7), $\mathcal A_1^m$, $\mathcal A_2^m$: standing assumptions. $\deg_a(i) = \sum_{j<i}a_{ji} + \sum_{j>i}a_{ij}$. By P011-T22, $n^2\widehat V_1(A;Z) = n\hat\sigma_\theta^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}\hat v_{ij}a_{ij}$ and $1^{\mathsf T}A1 = 2\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) The feasible set of the relaxation contains that of (3.6). (2) In (b): an integer feasible subgraph has at most one edge inside each group of three (every vertex has capacity one), so its positive weight is at most 2, and cross-sign edges have weight $-1$. (3) In (b), $n\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = \sum_i Y_i^2 = 6$ and $n = 6$. (4) The data of (b) are possible outcomes of a model satisfying the paper's assumptions (independent signs; any graph whose degrees are the recorded ones).
canonical_claim.note: Section 8 of the validator's derivation and exact_witnesses.json (keys rank_one_lp_gap, unit_weight_triangle). The reduction of P011-T13 does not make the paper's degree-only relaxation integral; this target records what the relaxation does give, which is what Proposition 3 needs for conservative inference (p. 2248).
